coach_says: d3 is a perfectly good move: it opens your c1 bishop and means ...e4 now just loses a pawn to dxe4. h3, asking the g4 bishop what it wants, was slightly more precise because it forces Black to trade it for your knight, but there's nothing to fix here.
also: question the pinning bishop with h3

coach_says: Kxf7 was the only move and you found it. Kf8 would have lost on the spot to Qd8+ Kxf7 Ng5 mate, so taking the bishop is both greedy and safe. You are a piece up; now get your king back to safety and develop.

This rook endgame against a bishop is lost whatever you do, and c4 is no worse than the alternatives. The most stubborn idea is to keep your pawns on light squares where your bishop can guard them and try to set up a fortress, but there is no real mistake to learn from in this move.

Your queen on b5 was attacked by the rook on d5, and Rc7+ dealt with that the clever way: check first, then move the queen next turn with your rook already on the seventh. You stay clearly winning. Just make sure you always notice when your queen is attacked before you play a check.
also: check before moving the attacked queen

coach_says: Bc4 against the Sicilian is playable but not ideal: Black can blunt the bishop with ...e6 and later ...d5, and then it is biting on a wall. Against 1...c5, developing a knight first with Nf3 keeps your options open (d4 or a quieter setup) before you decide where the bishop belongs.

a6 is fine. White can take on c6 and give you doubled pawns, but in return you get the bishop pair and a solid centre, which is a fair trade. Developing with ...Be7 or ...Nf6 was just as good; this is a matter of taste, not a mistake.

The game was already lost when you gave up your queen on move 10, and your knight on f5 is lost in every line. Nd4 does allow ...Qh4+ down the diagonal that f4 opened, so your king gets chased, but Ng7+ or the other tries end the same way. The real lesson is back on move 10, not here.

Rh2 is a good, natural plan: double your rooks on the open h-file and press on h5. It is as strong as the engine's own choices. Keep an eye on bringing the a4 knight back into play via b2 and d3 when you get the chance.
also: double rooks on the open file

coach_says: Your bishop on e7 was attacked by the queen and you had to deal with it, but on b4 it does nothing (the d2 pawn blocks the line to e1) and a3 kicks it again, so White gains time. Nc6 was better: it defends the bishop and brings a new piece into the game at the same time. When a piece is attacked, look first for a developing move that defends it.
also: piece kicked by a pawn loses time

coach_says: You missed Nd4! It attacks White's queen on b5, and the queen has almost nowhere to go: a5 and c5 are covered by your bishop, b4 by your queen, c4 by your d5 pawn and e2 by the knight. After Qd3 Nxf3+ Qxf3 Ba5 White's knight on a4 is trapped on the edge, because b6, c3 and c5 are all covered. Qc7 let White simply trade Nxb6 and escape; when an enemy queen and knight are short of squares, look for the move that hits them with tempo.
concept: trap the knight on the rim

coach_says: White was already threatening Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+, which moves the knight out of the way so the queen on d1 can take your bishop on g4. b5 attacks the c4 bishop, but it just takes on f7 with check, so you lose a pawn and your king. Nf6 was the move: it develops and protects the g4 bishop, so the trick stops working. Every time you pin a knight with ...Bg4, check whether that bishop is protected if the knight moves away.

f5 puts a pawn on the h3-c8 diagonal where White's bishop aims at your e6 rook and c8 rook. After Nxe6+ Nxe6 exf5 gxf5 Bxf5, your knight on e6 is pinned to the c8 rook, and White simply adds Re1 and wins it. Before pushing a pawn, check which lines it opens or closes for the enemy pieces; here ...Rce8 or ...Ree8 got your rooks off that diagonal first.
also: rooks lined up on a bishop's diagonal

coach_says: You spotted the threat Nc7+ forking your king and a8 rook, which is good, but you answered it by moving the king. Now your king has lost the right to castle and stays in the middle, and Nb6 comes in to hit your a8 rook and c8 bishop. Rb8 just moves the rook off the fork square; if Nc7+ anyway, Kd8 and the knight has nowhere useful to go (Nxa6 bxa6). When a fork hits your king and a piece, try moving the piece first.
concept: sidestep the fork with the rook
also: king stuck in the centre blocks development

coach_says: Your knight on g4 was attacked, but it was also blocking White's rook and queen on the g-file. When it retreated to h6, Rg6 hit your queen, and the queen has no good square left, so you lose it for a rook. You had a winning shot instead: Rxd4! cxd4 Qxd4+ with check, then the knight jumps in (Nf2+, Nd3+) to win the f4 bishop. When your piece is attacked, look for a forcing counter-attack before you retreat, and check what the retreat opens up.

You could have taken the knight on g7 for free: Rgxg7! and if fxg7, the f-file opens and Rxf1 is mate, because your rook on f7 was only blocked by that f6 pawn. Rg6 let the knight escape to h5. Whenever an enemy piece looks defended, ask whether the defender can actually recapture, or whether capturing exposes something behind it.

Kg2 walks onto a square the knight can fork: Ne1+ checks your king and hits your bishop on c2 at the same time, and you lose the bishop. Kf1 heads for the centre and covers e1 and e2, which is what the king wants in an endgame anyway. When a knight is near your king, check every square it can jump to before you move.

Your bishop on a3 is pinned: White's rook on a1 attacks it, and if it moves the rook takes your queen on a8. White was already threatening Bxe7, pulling the bishop away from the a-file. f6 chases the g5 bishop but ignores the pin and weakens e6, so Qe6+ comes in, and after Bc1 the pinned bishop falls. Qb7 was the fix: take your queen off the a-file and the bishop is no longer pinned.
also: weakened e6 and the g8 diagonal

coach_says: White is pushing g4 and h4 at your king, and Qe8 is a passive move that does nothing to slow that down. White's king is stuck on c2, so the better answer is c6, opening the centre and the c-file where White's king sits. When your opponent attacks on a wing, hit back in the centre rather than waiting.
concept: answer a wing attack in the centre
also: open lines at the enemy king

coach_says: Be7 is a passive retreat that leaves your knight on e8 tied up: after Be6+ Kf8 Bd7 White's bishop hits it and your queenside pawns start to drop. Qc5 was more active, putting your queen on the open c-file aiming at c1 and e3 near White's king, which keeps White busy. In queen endgames with an exposed enemy king, activity matters more than tidying up.

White was threatening Qh7 mate: the g6 pawn covers f7 and h7, and your own rook takes the f8 square. Qc5 ignores that and loses at once. Nf5, attacking the queen, was the move. Whenever an enemy queen and pawn get this close to your king, ask what they threaten before anything else.
